record.paper_title: Perspectivas sobre a Estatística de Extremos. Resultados básicos e problemas em aberto
record.original_question: In univariate extreme-value statistics, where a random sample is used to study maxima, minima, second maxima or minima, and exceedances of critical levels, how can the statistical-decision theory for extreme-value models be completed and extended beyond the already studied parts? In particular, develop methods for multi-sample analysis analogous to normal analysis of variance, Bayesian decision procedures, analysis of the effects of choosing the wrong model for the extreme-value distribution, and robust decision procedures, while also completing and extending partially developed work on estimation, hypothesis testing, prediction, discrimination, tolerance intervals, sequential analysis, and comparison of annual block-maxima methods with peak-over-threshold methods.

evidence.quote: De um conjunto (ou série) de observações aleatórias -a amostra- pretende-se estudar o comportamento estatístico do máximo ou do mínimo da amostra, do 2° máximo ou do 2° mínimo, a excedencia de um nível crítico, etc.

No que diz respeito à decisão estatística para extremos univariados estão muitos problemas em aberto, embora se já tenham resolvido alguns dos mais importantes -estimação/teste de hipóteses e predição com pequenas contribuições para a discriminação, intervalos de tolerância, análise sequencial, comparação entre o método dos máximos anuais (blocos) e o método P.O.T., etc.

Não só interessa completar os estudos mais avançados e alargar os apenas iniciados como abordar a análise multiamostras (análoga à análise de variância normal), a decisão bayesiana, os efeitos de modelização errada, a procura de decisão robusta, etc.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the univariate extreme-value setting in which one observes an i.i.d. sample $X_1,\dots,X_n$ from a distribution $F$ and is interested in the statistical behaviour of extreme order statistics — the sample maximum $M_n=\max_i X_i$, the sample minimum, the second maximum/minimum, and the exceedances of a high threshold $u$. Under classical extreme-value theory, suitably normalized maxima converge in distribution to a member of the generalized extreme-value (GEV) family
$$G_\gamma(x)=\exp\!\big(-(1+\gamma x)^{-1/\gamma}\big),\quad 1+\gamma x>0,\ \gamma\in\mathbb{R},$$
while exceedances over high thresholds are approximated by the generalized Pareto family. The basic statistical-decision problems for these models include point estimation of the shape, scale and location parameters; testing hypotheses about $\gamma$ (e.g. $\gamma=0$); prediction of future extremes; discrimination between members of the GEV family (Fréchet/Gumbel/Weibull domains); construction of tolerance intervals; sequential analysis; and comparison of the annual block-maxima method with the peak-over-threshold (POT) method.

Develop a complete statistical decision theory for univariate extreme-value models by accomplishing the following:

(a) Construct a multi-sample inferential framework analogous to the normal analysis of variance: given independent samples drawn from GEV (or generalized Pareto) distributions with possibly different parameters, design tests and estimators for equality of location/scale/shape parameters, with provable distributional properties (exact or asymptotic) and power analyses.

(b) Build a Bayesian decision-theoretic treatment for the GEV and generalized Pareto models, including the specification of objective and informative priors for $(\mu,\sigma,\gamma)$, derivation of posterior distributions and Bayes estimators/predictors under standard loss functions, and explicit decision rules for testing, prediction and tolerance intervals.

(c) Quantify the effects of model misspecification within and across the extreme-value families (e.g. fitting a Gumbel when the true law is GEV with $\gamma\ne 0$, or using block maxima when POT is appropriate), giving precise bias, variance and risk expressions for the resulting estimators, predictors and tests.

(d) Construct robust decision procedures for extreme-value inference that retain controlled performance under deviations from the assumed GEV/generalized Pareto model, including robust estimators of $\gamma$, robust predictive intervals, and a corresponding minimax or influence-function theory.

(e) Complete and extend the partially developed theory for estimation, hypothesis testing, prediction, discrimination, tolerance intervals, sequential analysis, and the formal comparison (in terms of efficiency and risk) between the annual block-maxima method and the peak-over-threshold method.

Provide unified theorems characterizing optimal decision rules in each of (a)–(e), together with their finite-sample and asymptotic properties.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is a broad research programme rather than a single conjecture. While significant progress has been made on individual components (e.g., Bayesian inference for GEV/GPD, robust estimators of the extreme-value index, model-misspecification studies, and block-maxima vs. POT comparisons in the modern extreme-value literature), no unified statistical decision theory completing all the listed items has been established. The overall programme thus remains open, with parts partially solved.

status_evidence.title: Statistics of Extremes: Theory and Applications
status_evidence.snippet: Comprehensive monograph covering estimation, testing and inference for extreme-value models, indicating substantial but incomplete progress on many of these decision-theoretic questions.
status_evidence.claim: Many of the listed sub-problems have partial solutions but no unified decision-theoretic completion.

status_evidence.title: Bayesian inference for extremes
status_evidence.snippet: Surveys Bayesian decision procedures for extreme-value models, showing the area is still under active development.
status_evidence.claim: Bayesian decision theory for extremes is partially but not fully developed.

status_evidence.title: Block maxima versus peak-over-threshold method
status_evidence.snippet: Compares efficiency of block-maxima and POT methods; recent work shows the comparison is still incomplete in generality.
status_evidence.claim: Formal comparison between block-maxima and POT methods is still an active open research topic.
